title: Sunlight warms things up
keyIdea: Sunlight warms the ground, the water and the things it shines on. A thing in the sun warms up more than the same thing in the shade, because shade is just a place where something blocks the sunlight. Dark things and sand warm up faster than white things and water, the ground is warmest in the middle of the day, and a roof that blocks the sun keeps a place cooler.

kid: The sun gives us light. It gives us warmth too. When sunlight shines on the ground, the ground gets warm.

Shade is a place where the sunlight is blocked. A tree, a roof or an umbrella can make shade. A stone in the sun gets hot. A stone in the shade stays cool. Shade does not make things cold. It just stops the sun.
Some things warm up faster. A dark T-shirt gets hotter than a white one. Sand gets hot fast, but water warms up slowly. That is why the sand can burn your feet while the sea feels cool.
In the morning the sun is low, and the slide is cool. In the middle of the day the sun is high, and the slide can be hot. A big umbrella can keep a spot cool.
adult: This matches two US kindergarten standards. K-PS3-1 asks children to 'make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface'. K-PS3-2 asks them to 'use tools and materials to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area'. At this age children compare warmer and cooler. They do not need to read degrees.

The science: sunlight carries energy, and a surface that takes it in warms up. Shade is where something blocks the direct sunlight, so less energy lands there. Warm air still warms shaded things a little. Dark surfaces take in more light than pale ones. Water warms more slowly than sand, as it needs more energy to heat and it mixes the heat down through its depth.

Common mistakes: thinking shade or a tree 'makes cold' instead of blocking sunlight, thinking the sun only gives light, and expecting a clear roof to keep things cool. Children also compare two things that differ in more than one way. The ground is often hottest in the early afternoon, a little after the sun is highest, as it keeps soaking up sunlight.

In the lab your child puts one stone in the sun and one in the shade and waits until midday. Next they compare a dark and a white can and feel sand and water. Then they drag the sun across the sky to warm and cool a slide, and test roofs until one keeps a dog's water bowl cool.

familyTip: On a sunny day, put two of the same toy outside, one in the sun and one in the shade. Feel them after lunch. Touch a dark car and a white car, or the sand and the sea, and talk about which is hotter and why. Then build a shade for a toy with a towel.

visual.caption: Does it get warm in the sun, or does it make shade? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: Blocks the sun to make shade

lab.caption: Flagship lab: compare sun and shade, dark and light, sand and water, follow the sun across the sky and build a roof that keeps water cool.

practice.prompt: Two toy cars sit outside. One is in the sun and one is in the shade. Which one gets warmer?
practice.hint: Think about which car the sunlight shines on.
practice.explain: Sunlight shines on the car in the sun and warms it. The shade blocks the sunlight, so that car stays cooler.

practice.prompt: A sandpit has 10 squares. An umbrella shades {a} of them. How many squares are still in the sun?
practice.hint: Start with all 10 squares and take away the shaded ones.
practice.explain: 10 − {a} = {=10-a}, so {=10-a} squares are still in the sun and will warm up more.

practice.prompt: There are {a} stones in the sun and {b} stones in the shade. How many stones will get hot?
practice.hint: Only the things the sunlight shines on get hot.
practice.explain: Only the {a} stones in the sun get hot. The {b} stones in the shade stay cooler, because the sunlight is blocked.

practice.prompt: Which T-shirt gets hotter in the sun?
practice.hint: Dark colours take in more sunlight than light colours.
practice.explain: The black T-shirt takes in more of the sunlight, so it gets hotter. The white one sends more of the light away.

pool.prompt: What does sunlight do to the ground?
pool.hint: Think of how a path feels after the sun shines on it all day.
pool.explain: Sunlight gives warmth as well as light, so the ground it shines on warms up.

pool.prompt: Why is it cooler under a tree on a sunny day?
pool.hint: What stops the sunlight from reaching the ground there?
pool.explain: The leaves block the sunlight and make shade. The tree does not make cold; it just stops the sun warming that spot.

pool.prompt: Sand and water sit in the sun all morning. Which feels hotter?
pool.hint: Think of the beach: the sand and the sea on a sunny day.
pool.explain: The sand warms up fast and feels hot. Water warms up slowly, so it feels cooler.

pool.prompt: When is a sunny slide hottest?
choices: in the middle of the day
pool.hint: When is the sun high in the sky?
pool.explain: In the middle of the day the sun is high and has shone on the slide for hours, so it is hottest.

pool.prompt: Which roof keeps a dog's water bowl cool in the sun?
pool.hint: The roof needs to stop the sunlight, not let it through.
pool.explain: An umbrella blocks the sunlight and makes shade. Clear plastic and a net let lots of sunlight through.

pool.prompt: You want to test if colour matters in the sun. Where should the dark can and the white can go?
choices: one in the sun and one in the shade
pool.hint: Keep everything the same except the colour.
pool.explain: Put both in the sun so only the colour is different. Then the dark can warms more, and you know colour did it.

pool.prompt: {a} children sit in the sun and {b} sit under a big umbrella. How many children are in the shade?
pool.hint: The umbrella blocks the sunlight. Who is under it?
pool.explain: The {b} children under the umbrella are in the shade. The {a} children in the sun will feel warmer.

pool.prompt: A path has 10 stones. A tree shades {a} of them. How many stones are in the sun?
pool.hint: Take the shaded stones away from all 10.
pool.explain: 10 − {a} = {=10-a}, so {=10-a} stones are in the sun and get warmer.
